description: Workers who are almost always employed are finding that seeking out a new role is a more daunting task.
fullText:
Workers who are usually employed have seen their job-finding rates fall sharply.

AI-exposed roles have seen the biggest drop in job-finding rates, reshaping the current job market.

Despite growth in some sectors, overall US job losses in July indicate ongoing labor challenges.

It used to be that if you're the type of person who always has a job, you're the type of person who can always find a job.

But a new analysis of job-finding rates complicates that picture. The study from the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond examines three types of workers and how they've fared in their job search.

"Primary workers," who make up about 55% of the US labor pool, are "almost always employed," per the analysis. They have steady work histories and usually only show up in unemployment statistics when something has gone wrong.

Historically, primary workers had the best odds of finding a new job. But their job-finding rates have fallen 13 percentage points from a November 2022 high to a September 2025 low — the biggest drop for any group the analysis covered.

Secondary workers, who make up about 14% of the labor pool, are often out of work or cycling through different jobs. They often make up the bulk of measured unemployment, and have a historically lower job-finding rate. While those workers still have a harder time finding jobs than their more attached peers, they haven't seen their fortunes fall as much; in the same period of November 2022 to September 2025, the job-finding rate for secondary workers fell just two percentage points.

This is new. In major recessions in the past, primary workers have seen their job-finding rates fall the most, followed by secondary workers. But now, primary workers are seeing that massive drop, while less secure secondary workers are not. So why would it be happening when the US economy is growing?

At the same time, the analysis finds that roles more exposed to AI — which the researchers define as the overlap of jobs' tasks with the capabilities listed in AI patents — have the biggest drop in job-finding rates. Before 2023, when ChatGPT became publicly accessible, job-finding rates for roles across levels of AI exposure moved together. Since then, outcomes have worsened dramatically for the AI-exposed fields.

AI has also shaken the hiring landscape for the new workers who might otherwise become strongly attached to the job market: As the report notes, research has found that generative AI can "substantially increase productivity at the task level (particularly for less-experienced workers), potentially altering the composition of new hiring."

title: Teacher busted under Kentucky's new anti-grooming law as advocate warns schools can't ignore red flags
description: Kentucky's new grooming law lands its first arrest after a school employee allegedly had an improper relationship with a minor student in Graves County.
fullText:
What can look like innocent attention toward a child can mask something far more sinister, a Kentucky advocate warns as the state's new grooming law lands its first arrest just weeks after taking effect.

Laura Wills-Coppelman, founder of ICKY, or Institutional Complicity Kentucky, told Fox News Digital that she sees the arrest as evidence of what the new grooming offense was designed to provide — an earlier opportunity for authorities to potentially intervene before alleged conduct escalates into sexual abuse.

"For the first time, Kentucky has a legal ability to intervene in a situation where a child could potentially face irreversible harm," Wills-Coppelman said. "It's a massive step forward in an effort to prevent child abuse."

Kentucky Middle School Teacher Accused Of Crossing The Line With Student, Arrested Under New Anti-grooming Law

The new law was invoked just weeks after taking effect July 15, when 25-year-old Sadie M. Flores of Mayfield was arrested and charged with grooming a minor, a Class D felony.

The Graves County Sheriff's Office said Flores, an employee at Graves County Middle School, allegedly had an improper relationship with a minor student in the district.

The allegation was initially reported to Graves County Schools, which immediately turned the information over to the sheriff's office, according to authorities.

Detectives seized electronic records, conducted interviews and took other investigative steps before interviewing Flores and arresting her around 3:30 p.m., the sheriff's office said.

High School Counselor Pleads Guilty To Multiple Sex Crimes Involving Teen She Was Meant To Help

Wills-Coppelman cautioned against drawing conclusions about Flores, saying the evidence and allegations in the case must now be evaluated through the court system.

But she said the arrest illustrates the significance of creating an earlier point at which authorities can investigate conduct that may precede abuse.

Wills-Coppelman said one of the biggest misconceptions about grooming is the belief that one questionable interaction can be viewed in isolation and labeled grooming.

Instead, she said grooming often unfolds gradually, with behaviors that may seem explainable on their own becoming increasingly concerning when they form a pattern.

"Grooming is a pattern of behavior that is intended to build trust, erode boundaries, and create conditions for a child to be exploited or abused," she said.

Potential warning signs, she said, can include excessive attention or favoritism, gifts, secrecy and increasingly isolating a child from other trusted adults or peers.

Individually, some of those behaviors may have innocent explanations. The alarm, Wills-Coppelman said, comes when adults begin seeing them develop into a broader pattern over time.

And from the child's perspective, she warned, grooming may not feel threatening at all.

Teacher Who Served As Gop State Lawmaker Allegedly Used Roblox To Lure Student Into Sexual Relationship

"Grooming is a form of manipulation," Wills-Coppelman said, explaining that a child may instead feel "special and seen and validated" by the attention.

"It doesn't often register as dangerous until it's too late," she said.

For parents watching from the outside, however, the same relationship may begin setting off alarm bells.

"Why does this adult need so much access? Why are they being isolated so much? Why so much excessive attention?" Wills-Coppelman said parents should ask themselves.

Wills-Coppelman said survivors her organization has spoken with have repeatedly described another troubling pattern — adults who recognized something felt wrong but did not speak up at the time.

"A lot of people, bystanders, in their situations in retrospect look back and say, 'I had an icky feeling,'" she said. "I saw something or I heard something that made me feel uncomfortable. I wish I would have spoken up."

She stressed that reporting concerning conduct is not the same as declaring someone guilty.

Instead, she said, authorities are responsible for examining the evidence and determining whether conduct meets the threshold for criminal charges.

"The point of awareness can be the point of prevention," Wills-Coppelman said.

That distinction has become particularly important amid concerns that ordinary interactions between teachers, coaches, youth leaders and children could be mistaken for grooming. The law makes clear that legitimate school, work and volunteer-related communications are not what it is designed to criminalize.

Wills-Coppelman rejected that characterization, calling appropriate adult-child boundaries "common sense."

"Healthy adult-child mentorship respects appropriate boundaries. Grooming erodes them," she said.

New Mississippi Law Expands Death Penalty To Include Inmates On Child Sexual Battery Convictions

"The intent of the law is to create an earlier intervention point, not to criminalize ordinary relationships between adults and children."

Wills-Coppelman said the legislation received unanimous support in both chambers of the Kentucky legislature and bipartisan backing.

House Bill 4, primarily sponsored by Republican state Rep. Marianne Proctor, passed the House 98-0 and the Senate 38-0 before the House unanimously approved the Senate's changes. Gov. Andy Beshear signed it into law April 10.

"This is not a political issue. This is a human issue," she said.

Ritzy Private Academy Attended By Kardashian Kids Faces Trial In Bizarre 'Kissing Club' Scandal

The pushback she has encountered, she said, has instead largely centered on due process and concerns about what happens after someone reports suspected grooming.

Wills-Coppelman said due process remains an essential part of the law because a report alone does not automatically trigger criminal charges. Investigators must evaluate the evidence before determining whether charges are warranted.

"We can preserve and respect due process and also prioritize the prevention of abuse and the protection of our children," she said. "They are not competing principles."

Wills-Coppelman said she ultimately hopes the law results not in more arrests, but fewer children ever reaching the point where alleged abuse occurs.

"The ultimate goal of this law is not more prosecutions," she said. "It's earlier recognition, awareness and understanding of what these behaviors look like and ultimately prevention."

For Wills-Coppelman, passing the grooming law is only one piece of a larger fight.

She said she now wants Kentucky's educator code of ethics brought into alignment with the new law and is pushing for greater accountability when people in positions of authority become aware of disturbing patterns but fail to report them.

That includes situations in which institutions attempt to handle serious allegations internally rather than referring them to the appropriate authorities, she said.

"My efforts are focused not only on the obvious villain, which is the perpetrator in these cases, but also turning some attention toward enablers, systems and institutions and the people within those organizations that had the capacity and the ability to take action and made a deliberate choice to not do so," Wills-Coppelman said.

In the Flores case, Graves County Schools said administrators contacted law enforcement immediately after becoming aware of the allegation.

Superintendent Matt Madding said the district has since been informed that charges were filed against the teacher and pledged continued cooperation with investigators.

"We take any allegation involving the safety of a child or the professional conduct of an employee extremely seriously," Madding said in a statement.

The district said it is limited in what it can disclose because the case remains an ongoing legal and personnel matter.

Wills-Coppelman hopes Kentucky's approach eventually reaches far beyond the state.

She said Ohio has legislation similar to Kentucky's, but her goal is for protections against grooming to ultimately become a nationwide standard.

"A child's protection from grooming and abuse should never depend on geography," she said.

For now, Kentucky's first case under the new law will move through the courts, while the legislation itself faces its first real-world test.

And for Wills-Coppelman, its success won't ultimately be measured by the number of people put behind bars.

"If it prevents even one child from the horrific consequences of abuse," she said, "that makes it all worth it."

title: Ken Paxton tries to tamp down growing Republican concerns about his Senate campaign
description: After years of battling fellow Republicans and helping lead the culture wars in Texas, Ken Paxton is campaigning on tax deductions, appearing with state lawmakers who once voted to impeach him, and op...
fullText:
After years of battling fellow Republicans and helping lead the culture wars in Texas, Ken Paxton is campaigning on tax deductions, appearing with state lawmakers who once voted to impeach him, and openly appealing to the Washington establishment for financial help.

It's all part of Paxton's efforts to unify his party after a bruising primary and pivot to a general election where he is already polling neck-and-neck with Democrat James Talarico. And it's an unusual position for Paxton, a veteran of intra-party fights in state races now waging a competitive general election that could determine control of the US Senate.

Texas Republicans are openly worried about losing a statewide race for the first time in three decades. Sen. Ted Cruz, who has been working privately to introduce Paxton to donors, recently said he expected the race "could be decided by a point or two," which would be tighter than Cruz's close call against Democrat Beto O'Rourke in 2018. And Michael Berry, a prominent conservative radio host, opened an interview with Paxton on Tuesday by saying he is in "a tough race."

"I know there is a lot of frustration. I hear it," Berry told Paxton. "What's the Paxton campaign doing? What's the path to victory? Let's talk about fundraising. I know that's been difficult. You beat a 24-year incumbent, obviously stepped on a lot of toes. There's been some concern. Will there be the money there to run the campaign it takes to win?"

Paxton has made significant inroads with Republicans in Austin and Washington, visiting DC recently for a fundraiser that was attended by Senate Majority Leader John Thune and other members. But it remains an open question how much outside funding Washington Republicans will pony up for the race – and whether Paxton and the GOP can unite enough to stave off a loss that could endanger the party's control of the Senate.

"We need help now," Paxton said in a Fox News interview Sunday, suggesting his campaign was trying to raise enough money so it could start airing TV ads next month.

Paxton is working to shore up support from Republicans after he defeated longtime Sen. John Cornyn in a May runoff with a late endorsement from President Donald Trump. The general election is unique in that neither Cornyn nor Rep. Jasmine Crockett, the Democratic primary runner-up, is actively campaigning for their party's nominee. But polling shows it is Paxton who trails Talarico in consolidating support from his party's voters.

Only a few House Republicans from Texas supported Paxton against Cornyn, but on Wednesday, Paxton's campaign touted that he now had the backing of 18 out of the 24 Republican members in the state's US House delegation – and that it signaled "unity."

Talarico has long staked his campaign on a populist economic message that cuts across party lines. He sought to set the tone for the rest of the election with a slickly produced rally last week in Arlington where he was introduced by Glen Whitley, who was a Republican when he served as Tarrant County judge from 2007 to 2022.

"We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis," Talarico said at the rally, blaming "billionaires buying politicians like Ken Paxton."

Talarico has also appealed to Cornyn supporters recently by praising the senator for sending a letter to the Trump administration raising concerns about border wall construction in Big Bend National Park. And after Paxton touted his latest congressional endorsements, Talarico's campaign issued a statement questioning why six House Republicans from Texas were still withholding their support. The group includes Reps. Michael McCaul, Dan Crenshaw and Chip Roy, all of whom are leaving the House after this year.

"I think that (Talarico's) got a chance with a small number of (Republican) voters – and he may only need a small number of voters," said Katherine Fischer, executive director of Texas Majority PAC.

Talarico has had a weekslong head start on TV advertising that his allies hope will help inoculate him from any coming ramp-up in GOP spending. Paxton has warned supporters that Talarico has gotten off to an early start in "trying to convince people that he's a moderate Democrat when he's not."

Talarico's campaign has spent $21 million on ads since the runoff compared to $100,000 by Paxton's campaign, according to AdImpact data. Even with an expected GOP ad blitz this summer and fall, a super PAC supporting Talarico, Lone Star Rising PAC, has yet to start seriously spending on his behalf. It had nearly $13 million in the bank heading into July.

GOP operatives in Texas and DC believe a group like the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races that worked hard to try to defeat Paxton in the primary election, or MAGA Inc., the pro-Trump super PAC sitting on $400 million, will ultimately need to spend big to get Paxton over the finish line.

One national GOP strategist who works on Senate races likened the situation to three Spiderman characters pointing at one another in a triangle.

"Everybody wants him to win, but nobody wants to go first," the strategist said.

A spokesperson for the Senate Leadership Fund, which is closely aligned with Thune, said in a statement that the group was "confident" Paxton would win but otherwise would not address any spending plans.

Paxton could be especially helped by the recent Supreme Court decision that struck down limits on coordinating spending between candidates and political parties. The National Republican Senatorial Committee pointed to that ruling when asked about the race for this story.

"The fall of coordinated spending limits means the NRSC can discuss spending decisions directly with our candidates and their campaigns," NRSC spokeswoman Joanna Rodriguez said in a statement. "The era of raising the curtain on strategy for press and the Democrats we're looking to defeat is over."

The chairman of the NRSC, South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott, brushed off concerns about Paxton in a recent interview with CNN's Manu Raju. Scott said the GOP's strategy for the race is "strong" and that it would be "very well-funded."

As for MAGA Inc., Scott noted the group recently briefed Senate Republicans on its plans for the midterms.

"We know that they're going to be fully engaged," Scott said.

Paxton has spent recent days campaigning on an economic plan that proposes new and increased tax deductions for health care, housing and children. In doing so, he has debuted rhetoric that is a stark departure from the red-meat sparring of the primary.

"Washington is making it harder than ever to get ahead, and the American dream is slipping away as the cost of everything, from housing to healthcare, rises," Paxton said in a video unveiling the economic agenda.

To be sure, Paxton' stump speech still features ample attacks on Talarico and his history of controversial comments on social issues, such as Talarico's 2021 declaration that "God is nonbinary."

He has been introduced at some events by some of his biggest intra-party detractors in the past.

One of them, at a Paxton stop in the Dallas suburb of Allen, was state Rep. Jeff Leach, who once called Paxton a "sophisticated criminal" and helped lead the 2023 impeachment against him in the Texas House on accusations of repeatedly abusing his office to help a donor. The Texas Senate acquitted Paxton.

Some of the GOP converts to Paxton have been more seamless than others. Paul Perez, head of the National Border Patrol Council, said it was an "easy and natural transition" to Paxton because the union already had a "longstanding relationship" with him even while supporting Cornyn previously.

"At the end of the day, it's bigger than a person," Perez said. "I think that's what everybody is looking at, is, 'How can we defeat the Democratic nominee?'"

After sitting out of the primary, one of Texas' top conservative donors, Tim Dunn, has started helping Paxton again after boosting him earlier in his political career. A super PAC funded by Dunn recently disclosed that it was spending $100,000 on text messages opposing Talarico.

The calls for Republican unity even extend to Texans for Lawsuit Reform, a pillar of the GOP establishment in Texas that Paxton has long vilified.

"Whatever difference Republicans have with each other, they pale in comparison to the abyss between common-sense policies around a strong economy and pro-consumer affordability vs the sharp leftward swing of the modern-day Democratic Party," the group's CEO, Ryan Patrick, said in a statement.

Among statewide officials, Gov. Greg Abbott has taken the lead on rallying Republicans since the primary, campaigning on a slogan of "Unity Drives Victory." Some Republicans hope the strength of Abbott's well-funded reelection campaign will help Paxton.

Not all Republicans are ready to embrace Paxton. Fort Worth Mayor Mattie Parker, a former Cornyn supporter and a top elected official in an important battleground county, remains neutral in the general election, a spokesperson confirmed.

Erik Gomez, mayor of the South Texas city of Sabinal and a prominent surrogate for Cornyn during the primary, is not ready to formally back Paxton. During the primary, Gomez questioned Paxton's ability to win in November and highlighted his personal issues, including Paxton's alleged extramarital affairs.

But Gomez said he was encouraged after a Paxton campaign staffer reached out a couple weeks ago. They plan to meet soon.

"That's a sign of a good gesture and good faith, reaching out to me," Gomez said. "I wasn't easy on the attorney general in my posts and on my campaign trail."

Gomez said he hoped he could speak with the Paxton campaign about some policy issues, its path to victory and unifying the party. He noted he still sees "Paxton supporters throwing jabs at Cornyn supporters."

"I personally want to see that stop," Gomez said.

title: Britain's Finlay Tarling dies in Volta a Portugal accident
description: British cyclist Finlay Tarling dies at the age of 19 in a serious accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.
fullText:
British cyclist Finlay Tarling has died aged 19 after an accident during the eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany-Ineos rider Josh, had raced for Great Britain on the road and track.

In a statement provided to local media, Major Tiago Machado of the National Republican Guard said there had been "a collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" and that an investigation was under way.

The Welshman was competing for the NSN Development Team when the incident occurred on the 166.8km route from Melgaco to Fafe.

In a statement, NSN said: "We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.

"Fin was a much loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed.

"Our deepest condolences go out to Fin's parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend."

In a post on X, the race organisers and the Portuguese Cycling Federation expressed their "most heartfelt condolences to the family of Finlay Tarling, to his team-mates, to the NSN Development Team, and to all his friends and loved ones".

It added that the racing was stopped and the scheduled podium ceremony would not take place as a sign of "respect and mourning".

Portuguese president Antonio Jose Seguro added that Tarling's death had "plunged the peloton, the tournament and the host nation into mourning".

British Cycling's performance director Stephen Park, added: "All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal.

"Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.

"Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time."

World governing body the UCI added on X: "The UCI is deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today's eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.

"The UCI extends its deepest condolences to Finlay's family, friends, and team-mates."

Meanwhile, the sport's governing body in Wales added: "We at Beicio Cymru (Welsh Cycling) are absolutely devastated to hear the news of Fin Tarling's passing today while competing at the Volta in Portugal.

"Fin was an incredible athlete, role model, friend, brother and son. We send our love and deepest condolences to Mike, Dawn and Josh at this incredibly difficult time.

"Rest in peace, Fin. You were incredible, and we will always remember you."

The Volta a Portugal got under way in Lisbon on 5 August and is raced over 10 stages, concluding in Porto on 16 August.

Tarling looked to be following in the footsteps of his older brother Josh as a time trial specialist.

He finished in third in the under-23 men's individual time trial at the British Championships in June and competed in the Tour of Britain just under 12 months ago.

title: Walter puts dominant Super Giants in Hundred final
description: All-rounder Paul Walter is the unlikely star with 80 off 46 balls as Manchester Super Giants comfortably beat Sunrisers Leeds to reach the men's Hundred final.
fullText:
The Hundred Eliminator, men's competition, The Kia Oval

Manchester Super Giants 186-4 (100 balls): Walter 80 (46). Klaasen 63 (26)

Sunrisers Leeds 166-7 (100 balls): Rickelton 54* (34), Brook 49 (31); Tongue 4-26

Paul Walter was the unlikely star as Manchester Super Giants beat Sunrisers Leeds by 20 runs in the Eliminator to cruise into the men's Hundred final.

Walter's 80 off just 46 balls set up Super Giants' imposing total of 186-4 at The Oval, before England seamer Josh Tongue led the bowling unit with an impressive 4-26 in Sunrisers' chase.

Having been put in to bat, Walter remained unflustered when opening partner Tim Seifert was dismissed from the second ball of the game, ensuring that Sunrisers' momentum was short-lived as he and Jos Buttler added 57 for the second wicket.

Buttler made 33 from 20 before Walter combined with the destructive Heinrich Klaasen and the pair added 114 off just 52 balls, with Walter whacking eight sixes and Klaasen four.

South African Klaasen blitzed a brutal 63 off 26 before he fell to Nathan Ellis.

Sunrisers have boasted one of the most powerful top orders in the tournament but struggled under the pressure of a mammoth run chase and they finished 166-7.

The tournament's leading run-scorer Mitch Marsh fell for 10 before captain Zak Crawley wasted a review when he was plumb lbw for six, which later proved costly as Harry Brook was given out lbw on 49 playing a reverse scoop - but replays showed the impact was outside the line of off stump.

Brook had shown glimpses of his brilliance in his 31-ball knock and was keeping Sunrisers' hopes alive, but his dismissal left them needing 89 off 44 balls and the innings fell away.

Tongue removed both Marsh and Crawley before he combined with Sonny Baker to tear through the middle order, the latter finishing with 2-39, while Sunrisers opener Ryan Rickelton was left stranded on 54 not out.

Super Giants will face Trent Rockets in the final at Lord's on Sunday.

Sunrisers defy superb Wong to reach Hundred final

Who am I? Guess The Hundred cricket star No 25

The Hundred 2026 tables, top run-scorers & wicket-takers

In a game featuring the likes of Buttler, Klaasen, Marsh and Brook, few would have predicted an Essex all-rounder would be taking the headlines.

Walter, 32, was picked up for just £31,000 in the auction earlier this year, a drop in the ocean compared to the £390,000 paid for London Spirit's James Coles.

He also did not even feature in Super Giants' first five games of the campaign before he came in at the top of the order after South Africa's Aiden Markram returned home for personal reasons, and has now finished with 225 in four games, averaging 76 and striking at 181.45.

It is a simple and unproblematic approach, but one that serves him well: 76% of all of his runs in this tournament have been scored on the leg side, and he reached his fifty off just 29 balls before Klaasen's followed off just 22.

Sunrisers' seamers continually bowled into his arc, and with the combined power between him and Klaasen, they had to hide their spinners. Liam Patterson-White's five balls were the only deliveries of spin bowled in the innings, while Super Giants were able to utilise Liam Dawson, Noor Ahmad and Michael Bracewell when their turn came.

Sunrisers needed an explosive start of their own from Marsh, and he started ominously with a six and a four in his first few balls before skying one high into the air for Baker to take a difficult, swirling catch.

Their hopes then lay with Brook, who played some outrageous shots of his own, including an upper-cut over the keeper to get off the mark and a lofted six over extra cover.

Crawley would have been wise to avoid eye contact with England's white-ball skipper knowing he burned the review that would have saved Brook.

title: Scheffler equals course record to lead first play-off event
description: Scottie Scheffler equalls the course record with a nine-under 61 as he opens up a three-stroke lead at the end of the second round of the St Jude Championship in Memphis.
fullText:
St Jude Championship - round two leaderboard

-11 S Scheffler (US); -8 Im (Kor), V Hovland (Nor); -7 L Aberg (Swe); -6 Nico Echavarria (Col), T Fleetwood (Eng), J Spieth (US), B Harman (US)

Selected others: -3 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), J Thomas (US); -2 A Rai (Eng); E H Hall (Eng); +1 S Lowry (Ire); +3 J Rose (Eng); +4 R McIlroy (NI), J Smith (Eng); +5 A Fitzpatrick (Eng)

Scottie Scheffler equalled the course record with a nine-under-par 61 as he opened up a three-stroke lead at the end of the second round of the St Jude Championship in Memphis.

The world number one, who already led the FedEx Cup standings heading into the first of three play-off events, birdied the first five holes at TPC Southwind.

The American proceeded to knock in a further six birdies, with bogeys on the eighth and 12th holes the only blemishes on his scorecard as he recorded his fourth career round of 61 or better on the PGA Tour.

"Really just a dream start. Probably one of the best starts I've had on tour, to be honest with you. I couldn't tell you a time where I've been lower early in the round," said Scheffler.

"My swing has felt really good in the past couple weeks, especially playing at home. It was nice to get out there and get things rolling early in the round and was able to keep the momentum going and shoot myself a nice round."

South Korea's Im Sung-jae is tied for second with Norway's Viktor Hovland at eight under overall, with Ludvig Aberg a shot further back.

Reigning FedEx Cup champion Tommy Fleetwood is the highest placed British player and in a quartet that also includes Jordan Spieth at six under.

Matt Fitzpatrick and fellow Englishman Aaron Rai, who collected his first major at the US PGA Championship in May, are at three under and two under respectively, with Northern Ireland's Rory McIlroy at four over.

With there being no 36-hole cut at any FedEx play-off event, six-time major winner McIlroy will hope to fare better over the weekend.

One player who will be absent though is Scotland's Robert MacIntyre, who withdrew prior to the start of play on Friday with a knee injury.

MacIntyre, who had limped to a 12-over 82 during the first round on Thursday, currently sits at 31st on the FedEx Cup points list.

The top 50 will head into next week's BMW Championship.

title: Trump says USS Lincoln's record time at sea during Iran operations 'not nearly long enough'
description: President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboar...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday downplayed the toll on American sailors enduring nearly nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln as concerns escalated about mental health and supply issues aboard the aircraft carrier supporting U.S. operations against Iran.

In a brief exchange with reporters before flying to New York for an event to highlight falling violent crime rates across the U.S., Trump refuted that family members have raised concerns about the deployment's length and even said that the deployment — which includes a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 240 days — is "not nearly long enough."

"That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it's being replaced with another very similar ship," Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. The acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, said the Lincoln "will return home soon" in a social media post on Friday.

Trump strode into office for a second term vowing to avoid lengthy and expensive military entanglements. And after launching the Iran war, alongside Israel, Trump and his advisers said the conflict would last a matter of weeks. The war is now more than five months old.

But on Friday, during his crime address in Garden City, New York, he acknowledged that he's used the U.S. military "a little bit more than I wanted to," while asserting anew that the U.S. operation against Iran is going well. He even said, seemingly in jest, that "pretty soon I'll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States."

"I'll never apologize," Trump added about the war and its impact on oil prices. "I did the right thing."

Extended deployments of carriers during the Iran conflict have raised concerns about the impact on service members who are away from home for long periods as well as the increasing strain on the ships and their equipment.

Several Democratic lawmakers, including Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, are pressing for accountability from the Pentagon over conditions aboard the Lincoln, which Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday said were "completely misrepresented."

Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., who served three tours in Iraq and Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division and 75th Ranger Regiment before being elected, took to social media to criticize Trump's comments, saying on X that "President Trump does not care about our servicemembers or their families."

Top Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have requested a classified briefing on the ship's food inventory, sanitation issues and healthcare availability, as well as an assessment of how much longer it would be deployed before relief arrives.

Republicans have been less outspoken about the situation on the Lincoln. The GOP chairmen of the House and Senate armed services committees did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

While hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have calmed in recent weeks, the Navy has reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports in the crucial Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war. Hegseth said the U.S. military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports "indefinitely."

Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week, and is expected to replace the USS Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.

After reports emerged that sailors on the Lincoln are struggling with mental health concerns, the Navy said it has "not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship," though officials have declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.

A Navy official said a sailor aboard the Lincoln went overboard in early August but the person was quickly recovered, treated by the ship's medical department and transferred off ship for follow-on care. The official would not say whether it was being considered a suicide attempt.

U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has also pushed back on reports about poor conditions.

AP writers Collin Binkley in Garden City, New York, and Michelle L. Price and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

This story has been corrected to show that the USS Abraham Lincoln has spent more than 240 days of uninterrupted time at sea and its overall deployment has exceeded 260 days.

title: The New Right’s Toxic Addiction to Racial Conflict

title: 'It's the economy, stupid' may solve Social Security woes, experts say
description: Social Security faces insolvency by 2032. Some experts say boosting the economy is the best antidote for Social Security's woes.
fullText:
Political strategist James Carville coined that phrase during Bill Clinton's 1992 presidential run against George H.W. Bush to remind Democrats to focus on pocketbook issues, but some analysts said that logic can also be applied to keep Social Security afloat.

The trust fund that supplements incoming payroll taxes to pay monthly Social Security benefits is expected to run dry by the end of 2032, according to the program's trustees. When that happens, the law requires benefits to be reduced by an estimated 22% to ensure the program's costs do not exceed its revenues.

While Congress has yet to raise taxes, cut benefits, or do both to keep affording payouts as population growth slows, some economists say the strongest Social Security reforms may not look like Social Security policy at all. Instead, they say, Congress should shift its focus to managing the economy better to encourage more Americans to work and earn.

"Social Security is a reflection of, and is supported by, the strength of the economy," said economist and Social Security expert Kathryn Anne Edwards at center-left think tank Roosevelt Institute. "Who is working, how much they earn, how healthy they are, and how much they save matter more than the head count. People could live longer, have fewer kids, and have a solvent Social Security if workers earned enough money."

Social Security is financed through a dedicated payroll tax. Employers and employees each pay 6.2% of wages up to $184,500 in 2026, while the self-employed pay 12.4%.

Now that the large Baby Boomer generation is retiring and collecting Social Security, and population growth has slowed, there aren't enough workers and payroll taxes to fully fund the benefits. That's resulted in the program dipping into its trust fund to make up for the shortfall and running down the balance.

Many politicians, including Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, and Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, support raising or eliminating the wage cap for the payroll tax to extend Social Security's solvency. Others have suggested raising the full retirement age from 67 years, increasing the payroll tax rate, or capping the annual cost-of-living adjustment.

People see Social Security as "the inexorable result of demographics," Edwards said. "This view stems from understanding Social Security as basically a pyramid scheme. Workers pay in, retirees get out, so the ratio between them underpins the program's stability. People live longer and have fewer kids, ergo, Social Security is running out of money. That's a one-dimensional view of a multidimensional problem."

title: 2 more states added to cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce
description: Cases linked to lettuce have now been documented in 17 states.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Two new states have reported an outbreak of cyclospora linked to lettuce, bringing the total number of affected states to 17.

Officials with the Food and Drug Administration added Maine and Massachusetts to the list in a Thursday update on the outbreak.

Cases of cyclosporiasis, the illness caused by cyclospora, have been confirmed in Arkansas, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maine, Michigan, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has tracked laboratory-confirmed 13,895 cases of cyclosporiasis since May 1, 2026, with 9,481 part of the outbreak. The total number of cases is likely to be higher because not everyone who is infected with cyclospora will see a doctor and because it requires specialized testing that may not be run for every person showing symptoms.

The outbreak has been linked to iceberg lettuce sold by Taylor Farms via Mexico, which was recalled on July 17. The best-by dates for the recalled products have passed, so it should no longer be available in stores or restaurants.

The FDA has initiated on-site inspections with the company, in cooperation with Mexican authorities.

Cases of cyclospora typically spike during the summer, as the parasite thrives in warm weather. However, the CDC has recorded a record number of cases this year, with some experts warning other produce could be affected as well.

Cyclospora is difficult to wash off produce, especially delicate items like berries and leafy greens or precut produce. It can cause explosive diarrhea and infections may persist as long as a month if not treated.

The Taylor Farms lettuce was distributed to restaurants and food service providers in Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Wisconsin and West Virginia.

The product may have been distributed to other locations, including California, the District of Columbia, Delaware, North Dakota, Puerto Rico, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont and Washington.

The recalled lettuce was also sold under the Marketside brand at Walmart stores in Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia.

The outbreak remains under investigation by the FDA and CDC.

FDA assigns highest-risk Class I status for recall of nearly 1.6 million cartons of eggs
description: A Class I recall indicates “a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death," accordin...
fullText:
(NEXSTAR) – A recall affecting nearly 1.6 million cartons of eggs has been assigned to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's most serious risk category.

The recall, which was initiated over concerns of potential salmonella enteritidis contamination, was categorized on Wednesday by the FDA as "Class I," indicating "a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of or exposure to a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death."

The new Class I designation was included in the agency's enforcement report for the existing recall.

The FDA has explained, however, that it often categorizes a recall well after the initiating firm makes the recall announcement, so it should not necessarily be viewed "as an expansion or change" to the firm's initial recall.

"Firms often initiate voluntary recalls and provide public statements or notifications as part of their commitment to protecting consumers, which may occur well before the FDA completes its classification process and subsequently posts to this report," the FDA said.

Midwest Poultry Services, of North Manchester, Indiana, first initiated its egg recall in July, announcing that 1,589,577 cartons of eggs (including white eggs and brown cage-free eggs) "have the potential to be contaminated" with the salmonella enteritidis bacterium. They were produced between June 6 and July 3 of this year and bear sell-by or best-by dates between July 20, 2026, and August 17, 2026.

The eggs were produced in Texas but shipped to multiple locations throughout the South and Southwest, including foodservice retail outlets in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Mexico, Oklahoma and Texas.

Among the outlets where the eggs were available were Kroger stores in Texas and Louisiana; Brookshire Grocery stores in Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico, and Mississippi, "and other smaller retail outlets," according to the initial recall alert.

The exact egg products that have been recalled are listed in Wednesday's enforcement report. Midwest Poultry Services previously urged consumers not to eat the eggs but to return them to the place of purchase for a refund.

No illnesses had been reported in connection with the recalled eggs as of late July.

Symptoms of salmonella infection often begin to show between six hours and six days after swallowing the bacteria, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Diarrhea, fever, vomiting and stomach cramps are common.

Those who believe they were infected are urged to contact a healthcare provider, especially if they are among the most vulnerable groups, or if symptoms worsen to include: bloody diarrhea (or diarrhea that lasts for more than two days); fever of over 102 degrees F; frequent vomiting that prevents the ingestion of liquids; and any sign of dehydration.

More severe illness linked to salmonella can include arterial infections, endocarditis (an infection in the heart), and arthritis. The infection is also blamed for 1.35 million illnesses and 420 deaths in the U.S. annually, according to the FDA.

title: El-Sayed’s half sister revealed as radical professor arrested for allegedly assaulting a cop at anti-ICE riot

fullText:
Controversial socialist Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is facing fresh scrutiny after it was revealed that his close relative is a far-left professor who was arrested on a felony charge last year for her role in an anti-ICE riot.

Eman Abdelhadi is a polarizing figure. She works as an associate professor at the University of Chicago's Department of Comparative Human Development, and has a years-long history of landing in the national spotlight for radical activism and inflammatory statements.

She's also El-Sayed's half sister.

Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-sayed Dodges Question On Whether He Still Supports Defunding The Police

She was charged on Oct. 3 with two counts of aggravated battery to a government employee, a Class 3 felony, and two counts of resisting/obstructing peace, a Class A misdemeanor.

A day before her arrest, she appeared on a podcast called "Movement Memos," which is affiliated with the far-left publication Truthout. During that interview, she recalled her previous experiences at the riots at the Broadview facility.

"These people are terrorizing our communities and they're setting up shop," she said, referring to federal immigration officials. "I mean, in Broadview, ICE has been setting up shop in our backyard. Just brazenly taking up community resources to terrorize this very same community."

"And so it felt really important to join protesters out there to say, not in our city, not in our name, not in our backyard," she added.

Progressive Michigan Senate Candidate's Staffer Raged At White Women In Unearthed Posts

Abdelhadi later expressed her frustration at establishment Democrats and claimed there is no wiggle room to accept centrist liberals in the left-wing.

"There's no center left," she said. "You're either resisting or you're complicit."

"The feeling when you think you've accomplished a lot but then your older brother runs for senate!!! In all seriousness—Abdul is fighting for healthcare, housing, and an economy that serves people over oligarchs. I am a proud little sister," she posted at the time to social media.

A profile of the candidate confirms Elkomy is El-Sayed's mother.

Abdelhadi's familial relationship with Elkomy is the subject of an independent film which explores her journey of coming out as queer in her traditionally Muslim family.

Abdul El-sayed Says Rallying With Hasan Piker Doesn't Mean He Endorses 'America Deserved 9/11' Remark

Fox News Digital reached out to Abdelhadi and El-Sayed's campaign, but did not hear back by time of publication.

Before her high-profile arrest, in July 2025, Abdelhadi made headlines for cursing out her employer at the Socialism 2025 conference. That conference is the largest annual gathering of collectivist leftists and describes itself as bringing thousands of "radical activists from around the country to take part in discussions about social movements, abolition, Marxism, decolonization, working-class history, and the debates and strategies for organizing today."

"F--- the University of Chicago, it's evil, you know it's a colonial landlord. Like, why would I put any of my political energy into this space? I kind of had a little bit of disdain for people who spent their time doing that," she said.

However, Abdelhadi reasoned that teaching there was her only chance to have any power.

Mamdani-backed Socialist Primary Winner Founded Group Whose Goal Is To 'Eradicate' Western Civilization

That's possible structural leverage," she said.

Despite her rant against the school and her subsequent criminal charges, the University of Chicago still employs Abdelhadi.

Abdelhadi also has a history of anti-White social media posts.

"Someday I'm going to make a twitter account called profoundwhiteguy and it will be the wisdoms of a basic white boy who thinks he's wise," she said in a 2017 post.

I kept thinking about how Muslims have been thrown off planes for speaking Arabic or 'looking scary'. But these women actually risking our lives were left alone," she said in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Abdul loves his sister and also disagrees with her on a number of political positions and the rhetoric she's chosen to use, including on foreign policy," campaign spokesperson Sophoie Pollok told Fox News Digital. title: Colombia says it will only accept rescue teams from four countries, as earthquake survival window closes
description: Hundreds are still missing as the crucial 72-hour window for rescues drew to a close on Thursday.
fullText:
Emergency teams in Colombia are searching desperately for survivors of an earthquake that has killed at least 281 people as the crucial window for rescues drew to a close on Thursday, with the government still only accepting help from a handful of countries.

Nearly 380 people are still missing, Colombia's agency for disaster preparedness and response said Thursday, after the quake damaged homes, schools, bridges and airports across a large swathe of the country.

"Our main efforts are focused on the missing," said President Abelardo De la Espriella in a statement late Wednesday, calling for unity.

Monday's devastating earthquake, the worst to hit Colombia in decades, posed an early test for the newly inaugurated leader. His government has surprised some by turning down or limiting help from several countries in the region, after they offered immediate assistance following the 7.4 magnitude quake.

On Wednesday, the newly appointed head for the disaster preparedness and response agency said the government would request rescue teams from only four countries: the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel. In Colombia's view, only those countries' rescue teams have the international and national certifications required for the job, said National Unit for Disaster Risk Management director David Tamayo Roldán.

Organizations including the United Nations and Mexico's famed "Topos" rescue brigade initially said they had not received a request for help with search and rescue. Aid agencies warn there is a critical 72-hour window after which the possibility of finding anyone alive in the rubble of collapsed buildings drops dramatically.

The Colombian Foreign Ministry has said it was preparing a list of "specific needs" to request international aid and that it had asked the United Nations Development Programme to provide support. In a statement, Foreign Minister Omar Bula also said that Colombia has "not excluded absolutely any country in terms of the offers that have been made to us," adding, "We work with countries without any ideological or political consideration."

Political scientist Sandra Borda linked the difficulties to the tense political transition between the current and previous administrations and said the new government showed "a deep distrust of some parts of the international community," which she considered "difficult to understand."

She added that there was "no clarity about the procedure that was to be followed."

"There was a perception from the beginning that the rescue teams would be sufficient, although a technical assessment was never made public to confirm that they would indeed be enough to deal with all the damage and destruction caused by the earthquake," she said.

It has also been unclear where international personnel are needed. The emergency chief of the fire department in Cali, one of the most affected cities, warned volunteers not to approach collapsed sites "because there are already enough specialized personnel to carry out the rescue work without complications."

The Topos Tlatelolco Rescue Brigade, a Mexican group with extensive experience responding to natural disasters, said Wednesday that Colombian authorities "will not allow the entry of external rescue groups" because the work is being handled by national rescuers.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed that her government was in contact with Colombia, but said its government had not given its approval to rescuers, who were "ready to leave at any moment."

"We are sending, via Hercules planes, food supplies, medical supplies, and other things they've requested. But yes, just to clarify: the rescue brigade from the Secretariat of National Defense was not approved by the Government of Colombia," she said.

Meanwhile, in Pereira, one of the most severely affected cities, the foreign ministry celebrated the arrival of 19.5 tons of aid from Mexico.

"Additional flights are expected in the coming days. Colombia is not alone! The international community is with us," the ministry said on X.

Michael Rios contributed to this report.

title: RFK Jr. says he’s seen ‘boxes and boxes’ of McDonald’s on Trump plane
description: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a new interview said he’s seen “boxes and boxes” of McDonald’s food while traveling on Air Force One with President Trump, who he said eats...
fullText:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in a new interview said he's seen "boxes and boxes" of McDonald's food while traveling on Air Force One with President Trump, who he said eats fast food because he's worried about food poisoning.

"When you get on his airplane, it's just boxes and boxes of McDonald's," he said during an appearance on the "Net Positive" podcast.

One of the hosts, John Crist, asked Kennedy if he ever tried to correct Trump's diet or if it conflicted with the secretary's agenda.

"I'm not like a scold," Kennedy responded. "He eats really good food most of the time, but when he's traveling, he likes to eat food from national chains because he's scared of getting food poisoning."

"When he's at Mar-a-Lago or the White House, that's the best food; it's all fresh produce, and a lot of it is locally sourced. So he is eating good food most of the time," he added.

Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz also joked in February about other items in Trump's diet.

"Your dad argues that diet soda is good for him because it kills grass. It's poured on grass, so therefore must kill cancer cells inside the body," Oz told Donald Trump Jr. on "Triggered," the president's son's podcast.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt laughed the comment off and said she heard the president also make the same joke.

Kennedy has gained public attention for his diet centered on fermented foods and grass-fed meat. White House officials have joined him on this regime, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Vice President Vance.

Kennedy credited the diet for helping him lose 20 pounds in 30 days and easing issues with an irregular heartbeat. Former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) said he lost 4 inches off his waist after adopting the plan.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday called Kennedy's diet "crazy."

He added that the diet was not for everyone and he encouraged people to try it out.

title: MN Senate candidate ripped for blaming Walz for fraud despite being his #2: 'Knows she's cooked'
description: Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan pointed the finger at Tim Walz when asked about her responsibility for the massive fraud scandal.
fullText:
Minnesota Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan pointed the finger at Gov. Tim Walz when asked during a recent interview about her responsibility for the massive fraud scandal that unfolded under their watch.

"I would say, the governor says the buck stops with him, more should have been done sooner, and I agree," Flanagan said on MSNOW on Thursday when asked if she bears any responsibility for the scandal, which federal investigators have said could total more than $9 billion.

Flanagan, who is the Democratic nominee for Senate in Minnesota, continued, "And now we know that 100 people have been charged, 60 have been convicted."

Flanagan's comments sparked pushback on social media from users accusing her of deflecting responsibility given she has served alongside Walz as his second in command since 2019.

Peggy Flanagan Was Minnesota's No 2 Official As Massive Fraud Scandal Exploded Under State's Watch

"Minnesota Democrat Peggy Flanagan blames Tim Walz and dodges accountability for rampant fraud in her state," the Republican National Committee (RNC) posted on X.

"She KNOWS she's vulnerable on this," conservative radio host and editor Larry O'Connor posted on X. "Huge opening for @Michele_Tafoya."

Former sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, Flanagan's Republican opponent in November, also reacted to the clip in a post on X saying, "Peggy Flanagan refuses to take any responsibility and accountability for billions of our tax dollars being stolen under her watch as lieutenant governor.

Hall Of Famer Tony Dungy Endorses Michele Tafoya In Crowded Minnesota Republican Primary For U.s. Senate

"Minnesotans deserve better than excuses. They deserve leaders who will take responsibility and get the job done."

Townhall columnist Dustin Grage posted on X, "Here is Peggy Flanagan blaming Tim Walz for the fraud. Oh yeah, she knows she's cooked if she rightfully gets tied to the fraud."

The fraud scandal in Minnesota ultimately pushed Walz to drop his bid for re-election, and critics have continued to hammer his administration for not doing enough to prevent the growing fraud problem, which had become an open secret in the state over the past few years.

Flanagan's culpability in the fraud scandal will likely become a major talking point in her campaign for Senate as calls from conservatives for more accountability continue to pour in as no top officials have been fired or removed from office in the scandal's aftermath.

"@peggyflanagan did NOTHING to protect vulnerable citizens & taxpayers despite countless whistleblower reports, Auditor reports, & criminal convictions," Minnesota Republican State Rep. Kristin Robbins, who chaired the Minnesota House's Fraud Prevention and Oversight Committee posted on X this week.

"Peggy Flanagan, @Tim_Walz & @keithellison protected their political base instead of stopping the fraud.

Flanagan did not mention fraud during her victory speech following Tuesday night's Senate primary, which also drew criticism from Tafoya on social media.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Flanagan campaign for comment.
